## TL;DR

I ran the Debug → Logs view through a headless browser at the requested desktop
and phone widths, including a 1,000-row payload, an unbroken 12,000-character
log title, expanded detail, and a failed logs request. The page did not extend
past the viewport and did not throw browser exceptions. I tightened line
wrapping and log block sizing, and added a regression test that preserves the
full long message and detail when expanded.

## Work and rationale

The first pass used the existing `drawer:debugLogs` fixture. At both 1280 px and
375 px, its remote warning, long log entry and short completion message fit the
viewport. This provided a baseline for the real Debug → Logs layout, but it was
not enough to cover the unusually long content named in the task.

I then routed `/api/tasks/1198/logs` to a local response containing 1,000 log
entries. Each entry included a long URL-like token, and the first entry included
a 2,000-character context value. The task drawer also showed three existing
activity events, for a total of 1,003 rendered event rows. At both requested
viewport widths, `document.documentElement.scrollWidth` matched `innerWidth`.
The expanded output block also stayed inside its parent: 615 px wide on desktop
and 322 px wide on mobile, with no internal horizontal scroll. No page errors
were recorded.

The component already preserved the full content in Vue, but its CSS relied on
`word-break: break-word` in the preformatted output and messages. I changed
those blocks to `overflow-wrap: anywhere`, which explicitly handles long
identifiers that contain no natural break points. The output block now has a
border-box maximum width and can shrink within its parent. Event titles also
allow arbitrary wrapping at narrow widths, which makes long tokens readable
instead of merely clipping them. This is limited to the DebugPanel's rendered
content and does not change the stored log or activity data.

The regression test creates a log message with a 12,000-character unbroken
token and a 2,000-character context string, expands it, and checks that the
complete message and context remain rendered. The empty/error browser pass
returned HTTP 500 for the logs request, then filtered to Logs. The non-fatal
fetch path displayed “No debug events yet.”, with no page-width overflow or
browser exception. The interface currently treats that failed request like an
empty result; I recorded that behavior rather than changing the store's error
contract as part of this rendering-focused pass.

## Approaches tried

I started with the existing preview fixture because it provides real app data
without changing task logs or requiring task-specific backend setup. After
that, I intercepted the logs endpoint in headless Playwright to create a
repeatable stress payload. This exercised the actual running app, drawer,
filters and component styles, rather than relying on a static HTML mock. I
measured document width and the expanded pre block at both viewport sizes, and
checked for page exceptions. The 1,000-row run completed with every row
rendered; I did not add list virtualization because this pass did not reproduce
a freeze or unacceptable render delay at the requested sizes.

The component test is separate from the browser measurements: it verifies that
long output is retained by the component after expansion. The UI build checks
the scoped style and TypeScript changes. The scoped RepoOS check is the final
gate for this branch.

## Challenges and blockers

The task's preview fixture covers representative log and remote-event shapes,
but it does not provide an oversized payload. I used a Playwright route mock
for that case and ensured it existed only in the browser session. The mock
returned 1,000 rows, so this is evidence about rendering volume and viewport
fit, not evidence about a real task that has accumulated that many logs.

The logs API request handles errors non-fatally, and the DebugPanel uses the
same empty-state copy for an empty result and a failed fetch. The task asks for
empty and error states to render without overflow or lag; both conditions did
render cleanly. Making the failure state distinct would require an explicit
store error state and a product decision about its user-facing copy, so I did
not broaden this change beyond output wrapping.

No visible browser or user Chrome was used. The app was served with
`just serve-noauth 7289` from the task worktree, and the Playwright browser ran
headless against that server.

## Key learnings

The panel's normal fixture was already responsive, so the decisive cases were
long unbroken identifiers and an expanded context block. Checking only
`documentElement.scrollWidth` would miss content clipped inside a scrollable
block; I measured the block's own client and scroll widths too. A 1,000-row
render remained responsive in the observed run, so eager rendering did not
justify introducing a more complex virtual list. The regression test now keeps
the long-content expansion behavior visible to future changes, while the QA
record describes exactly which parts used mocked data and what was actually
observed.
